column5: singing to YHWH; blessing the Name day by day
column6: The psalm commands singing to YHWH, blessing his name, and proclaiming salvation from day to day; it supplies a distinct psalmic formulation of the commentary's vocal praise, Name, recitation, and recurring practice.

column5: thanksgiving, praise, blessing the Name
column6: Entering God's courts entails thanksgiving and praise, then giving thanks to him and blessing his name. The verse closely joins the commentary's dhikr as praise and thanks with public worship of the Name.

column5: not forgetting God's word
column6: The psalmist vows not to forget God's word; this is a direct, text-specific counterpart to the commentary's recitation, non-forgetting, and later reminder within the surah's devotional sequence.

column5: lips pouring out praise after instruction
column6: The psalmist's lips pour out praise because God teaches statutes. It specifically joins a tongue-level act of praise to received teaching, as the commentary joins Qur'an recitation and dhikr.

column5: tongue singing God's word
column6: The psalmist's tongue sings God's word; this is a precise oral-scriptural parallel to the commentary's statement that reading the Qur'an belongs to remembrance.

column5: prayer as incense; lifted hands as evening offering
column6: Prayer is likened to incense and raised hands to the evening offering. It supplies a concrete bodily and time-marked analogue to the commentary's prayer as supplication and enacted worship.

column5: house of prayer; accepted offerings
column6: God's house is called a house of prayer for all peoples, where offerings are accepted. This directly pairs prayer with formal communal worship, an important aspect of the commentary's unified tesbih, dhikr, and salat.

column5: lifting heart with hands to God
column6: Lamentations calls for lifting both heart and hands to God. The explicit union of inward disposition and visible bodily action sharpens the commentary's word-action-intention account of prayer.

column5: standing before the altar; spreading hands toward heaven
column6: Solomon stands before the altar in the assembled people's presence and spreads his hands heavenward. It supplies a specific biblical prayer posture alongside the commentary's standing and supplicatory movements.

column5: supplication heard; divine forgiveness
column6: Solomon asks God to hear prayer and supplication and to forgive. The verse gives a direct biblical meeting between human du'a-like appeal and the divine cleansing or forgiveness side of the commentary's 14–15 linkage.

column5: evening offering; kneeling; spread hands
column6: At the evening offering Ezra rises from his self-affliction, falls to his knees, and spreads his hands to God. Its timed and bodily prayer scene closely meets the commentary's descriptions of salat.

column5: voice of thanksgiving; sacrifice; vowed act
column6: Jonah promises sacrifice with a voice of thanksgiving and the fulfilment of vows. This compactly combines vocal praise, gratitude, ritual action, and obedience, all senses the commentary assigns to dhikr and tesbih.

column5: God sprinkling clean water and cleansing
column6: Ezekiel depicts God cleansing the people from impurity. It does not itself define prayer, but it supplies the divine purification pole required by the commentary's linking of 87:14 to God's purifying salat.

column5: whole heart and voice; blessing the Lord's Name
column6: Ben Sira tells hearers to give thanks with all heart and voice and bless the Lord's name. It is an unusually close Jewish synthesis of inward intent, vocal praise, and the Name.

column5: service of the heart interpreted as prayer
column6: The Talmud asks what service is performed with the heart and answers, prayer. This interpretation directly illuminates the commentary's claim that worship includes intention as well as its audible and bodily forms.

column5: a blessing requires God's Name and kingship
column6: The rule that a blessing without the Name and kingship is no blessing makes formal invocation of the divine Name a defining liturgical act, a useful rabbinic counterpart to 87:1 and 87:15.

column5: public Torah and Shema recitation in temple liturgy
column6: The daily temple order combines blessings with recitation of Torah passages and the Shema. It gives a concrete Jewish liturgical setting for the commentary's claim that scriptural reading is part of remembrance and worship.

column5: public prayer performed to be seen
column6: Jesus criticizes prayer offered for public display. In conjunction with the commentary's treatment of jahr as audible prayer, it makes intention rather than volume the relevant ethical distinction.

column5: vain worship through human teaching
column6: The continuation of Jesus' Isaiah citation calls worship vain when it teaches merely human precepts. It gives the explicit Christian continuation needed for the commentary's concern with heedless or merely external worship.

column5: prayer before dawn
column6: Jesus rises while it is still dark and prays in a solitary place. This is a specific Christian scene for the commentary's praise and prayer before the sun's rising.

column5: the people praying at the hour of incense
column6: The whole assembled multitude prays outside during the incense hour. It offers a precise communal and timed liturgical counterpart to the commentary's formal prayer practice.

column5: night-and-day service with fasting and prayers
column6: Anna serves God night and day through fasting and prayers. Her recurring discipline meets the commentary's abundant remembrance and continuing worship without reducing it to one isolated prayer.

column5: prayers and alms as a memorial before God
column6: Cornelius's prayers and alms ascend as a memorial before God. The passage gives a striking New Testament link between remembrance, prayer, and obedient action, matching the commentary's broad account of dhikr.

column5: washing away sins while calling on the Name
column6: Paul is told to be washed from sins while calling on the Lord's name. It specifically joins name-invocation to cleansing, a close Christian meeting of the commentary's remembrance and divine purification relation.

column5: secrets of the heart; falling face-down; worship and confession
column6: When hidden heart-secrets are disclosed, the hearer falls on his face, worships God, and declares God truly present. This unusually combines the commentary's hidden/open axis, prostration, and voiced God-remembrance.

column5: every tongue confessing to God's glory
column6: The verse completes the preceding knee-bending with every tongue's confession to the glory of God the Father. It gives the verbal side of the name-and-body meeting already present in the commentary.

column5: word and deed in the Name; thanksgiving
column6: Whatever is done in word or deed is to be done in the Lord's name with thanks. This directly mirrors the commentary's integration of utterance, deed, Name, and gratitude under worship.

column5: supplications, prayers, intercessions, thanksgivings
column6: The verse deliberately lists supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings. It supplies a close Christian comparison to the commentary's semantic expansion of salat and dhikr into du'a, praise, and thanks.

column5: prayer everywhere; lifted holy hands; moral restraint
column6: The instruction to pray everywhere with lifted holy hands is joined to rejection of anger and disputing. It connects the commentary's bodily prayer with its ethical claim that prayer opposes wrongdoing.

column5: drawing near; hearts sprinkled clean; bodies washed
column6: Hebrews couples approach to God with a true heart and imagery of cleansed hearts and washed bodies. It provides a Christian purification-and-worship analogue to the commentary's 87:14–15 association.

column5: falling in worship; harps; bowls identified as prayers
column6: The elders fall before the Lamb while holding harps and bowls of incense identified as the saints' prayers. This heavenly liturgy joins body, praise music, and prayer in a form especially relevant to the commentary's single devotional practice.

column5: glorifying the Name and worship by all nations
column6: The hymn asks who would not glorify the Lord's name and says all nations will come and worship. It directly pairs name-glorification with worship in a Christian doxological formula.

column5: Lord's Prayer formula; hallowing the Name
column6: The Didache transmits the Lord's Prayer as the form believers are to pray, including the hallowing of the Father's name. It supplies the early Christian liturgical text that its following thrice-daily rule presupposes.
